noun:Japanese.tx: From Japan + -ese, after the model of earlier Portuguese japonês, New Latin japonensis, etc.

adv:je.tx: From Middle High German ie, from Old High German io.

noun:Johannisbeere.tx: Johannis + Beere, literally “John's berry”, named for the feast day of St. John the Baptist (24th of June), said to be when the fruit ripens.

adv:jedoch.tx: From Middle High German iedoch, idoch, ēdoch, from Old High German iodoh, iothoh. Equivalent to je + doch. Compare Dutch edoch.

conj:jedoch.tx: From Middle High German iedoch, idoch, ēdoch, from Old High German iodoh, iothoh. Equivalent to je + doch. Compare Dutch edoch.

adv:just.tx: Derived from Latin iūste, iūstus, perhaps via Middle Dutch juust.

adv:ja.tx: From Middle High German ja, from Old High German ja, jā (“yes”), from Proto-Germanic *ja (“yes”). Cognate with Yiddish יאָ (yo).

intj:ja.tx: From Middle High German ja, from Old High German ja, jā (“yes”), from Proto-Germanic *ja (“yes”). Cognate with Yiddish יאָ (yo).

intj:jo.tx: Alteration of ja (“yes”) or the respective dialectal cognates. Compare English yo, Swedish jo.

intj:jawohl.tx: Univerbation of ja (“yes”) and an emphatic wohl (“well, certainly”). Compare Dutch jawel.

adj:jüdisch.tx: From Middle High German jüdisch (judisch, jüdesch, judesch), from Old High German judeisc, derived from judo, judeo + -isc, the former from Latin iūdaeus (“Judaean, Jew”), from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), derived from Ἰουδά (Ioudá, “Judah”) + -ιος (-ios), the former from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (yəhūḏāh). By surface analysis, Jude + -isch. Doublet of jiddisch.

noun:Junge.tx: Fixed nominalisation of Middle High German jung (“young”), from Old High German jung (“young”). Already occasionally in Middle High German [Term?], later gaining a fixed noun form based on its weak nominative inflection (giving ein Junge instead of ein Junger). The recognition as the normal standard term for “boy” is based on Central and Low German usage and has only fully asserted itself during …

pron:jener.tx: From Middle High German jener, from Old High German jenēr, from Proto-West Germanic *jain, from Proto-Germanic *jainaz. Cognate with English yon.

noun:Jacht.tx: From Dutch jacht (“yacht”), a reduction of jachtschip (literally “chase ship”). The spelling Yacht became standard in German under English influence, though it has now become less common again. For more, see English yacht (also borrowed from Dutch). Doublet of Jagd.

noun:Jade.tx: From French jade (“jade”), rebracketing of earlier l'ejade (“jade”), from Spanish piedra de ijada (“flank stone”), from Vulgar Latin *iliata, from Latin ilia (“flank”) (Jade was thought to cure pains in the side).

noun:Jaguar.tx: Borrowed from Portuguese jaguar, from Old Tupi îagûara.

noun:Januar.tx: Learned borrowing from Latin Iānuārius. Doublet of inherited Jänner.

noun:Judas.tx: From Latin Judas, from Ancient Greek Ἰούδας (Ioúdas), from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (yəhūḏā).

noun:Juni.tx: From the Latin (mēnsis) Iūnius (“[month] of June”).

noun:Junker.tx: From Middle High German juncherre (“young lord, not yet knighted nobleman”); a reduced form of a compound of the equivalents of jung (“young”) and Herr (“lord”). Compare similarly constructed and reduced Jungfer. Cognate of Dutch jonkheer, jonker.

noun:Jute.tx: 19th-century borrowing from English jute with a spelling pronunciation. Eventually from Sanskrit जूट (jūṭa, “twisted hair”).

noun:Jahr.tx: From Middle High German jār, from Old High German jār, from Proto-West Germanic *jār. Compare Low German Johr, Jahr, Dutch jaar, English year, Danish år. Doublet of Uhr.

noun:Jammer.tx: From Middle High German jāmer, from Old High German jāmar, from Proto-West Germanic *jāmar, from Proto-Germanic *jēmaraz. Cognates include Dutch jammer and English yammer.

verb:jammern.tx: From Middle High German jāmern, jāmeren, from Old High German jāmarōn, from Proto-West Germanic *jāmarōn, from Proto-Germanic *jēmarōną. Compare English yammer.

adv:jetzt.tx: From Middle High German iez, ieze, iezū, iezō, iezuo, from Old High German iozuo (“straightaway, at once; further”), equivalent to je + zu. Compare English yet, Yiddish יעצט (yetst).

verb:jagen.tx: From Middle High German jagen, from Old High German jagōn, from Proto-West Germanic *jagōn.

noun:Johannes.tx: From Medieval Latin Jōhannēs, from Late Latin Iōhannēs, variant of Latin Iōannēs, from Koine Greek Ἰωάννης (Iōánnēs), from Biblical Hebrew יוֹחָנָן (Yôḥānān) (perhaps from a former J^əhôħānān). Cognate with English John.

noun:Jude.tx: Inherited from Middle High German jude, jüde, from Old High German judo, judeo, from Latin iūdaeus (“Judaean, Jew”), from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), derived from Ἰουδά (Ioudá, “Judah”) + -ιος (-ios), the former from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (yəhūḏāh).

adj:jung.tx: From Middle High German junc, from Old High German jung, from Proto-West Germanic *jung, from Proto-Germanic *jungaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yuh₁n̥ḱós. Compare Dutch jong, English young, Danish ung.

noun:Joch.tx: From Middle High German joch, from Old High German joh, from Proto-West Germanic *juk, from Proto-Germanic *juką, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm.

noun:Jugend.tx: From Middle High German jugent, from Old High German jugund, from Proto-West Germanic *jugunþi, from Proto-Germanic *jugunþiz. Akin to Old Saxon juguth, English youth.

prep:jenseits.tx: From Middle High German jensīt, ensīt, equivalent to jene (“that”) + Seite (“side”) + -s (adverbial suffix). Cognate with German Low German güntsied, güntsiet, güntsieds, güntsiets, Saterland Frisian junsiede.

adv:jenseits.tx: From Middle High German jensīt, ensīt, equivalent to jene (“that”) + Seite (“side”) + -s (adverbial suffix). Cognate with German Low German güntsied, güntsiet, güntsieds, güntsiets, Saterland Frisian junsiede.

noun:Jacke.tx: From Middle French jaque, originally a peasant garment, from the name Jacques (“James”), considered a typical peasant's name.

noun:Jagd.tx: From Middle High German jagit, jaget, jagāt, from Old High German jagōd, from Proto-West Germanic *jagōþu. Doublet of Jacht.

noun:Jauche.tx: Borrowed from Middle Low German juche, from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *jūxà, from Proto-Balto-Slavic *jáušāˀ, from Proto-Indo-European *yowHs-ó-s, from *yéwHs. Compare Lower Sorbian jucha, Polish jucha, and Serbo-Croatian juha. Doublet of Jus.

noun:Jause.tx: From Middle High German jūs, from Slovene júžina (“lunch”).

adj:jäh.tx: From Middle High German gǣhe, gāch, gā (“quick”), from Old High German gāhi (“sudden, quick, rash”), from Proto-Germanic *ganhuz, *ganhwuz (“sudden”). The modern onset j- is from a Central German dialect. Other dialects have brought forward forms such as gäh, gäch or gach (obsolete in standard usage), compare Bavarian gach. Cognate with Dutch gauw (“soon”). More at gay.

verb:jucken.tx: From Middle High German jucken, jücken, from Old High German jucchen, from Proto-West Germanic *jukkjan. The form with -u- reflects (chiefly Upper German) umlaut hindrance before a velar geminate; here likely reinforced by the desire to avoid jü- (which exists only in derivatives of jung and Jude; cf. also the total absence of ji-).

verb:jäten.tx: From Middle High German jeten, from Old High German jetan, from Proto-Germanic *jedaną.

pron:jeder.tx: From Middle High German ieweder, from Old High German ioweder, from io + wedar. Compare English either, Dutch ieder. Around the 14th century, the word merged with ieder, at which point the dual sense, "both", died out.

det:jeder.tx: From Middle High German ieweder, from Old High German ioweder, from io + wedar. Compare English either, Dutch ieder. Around the 14th century, the word merged with ieder, at which point the dual sense, "both", died out.

noun:Jungfrau.tx: From Middle High German juncvrouwe, from Old High German juncvrouwa (“maiden; unmarried noblewoman”). Equivalent to jung + Frau. Compare Danish jomfru, Dutch jonkvrouw (“maiden”), juffrouw (“unmarried young woman; female teacher, nanny”), Yiddish יונגפֿרױ (yungfroy).

noun:Jürgen.tx: Derived from Low German, from Middle Low German Jurian (compare Dutch Jurriaan, Swedish Örjan), from Latin Geōrgius (which see for cognates), from Ancient Greek Γεώργιος (Geṓrgios), whence also Georg, Jörg.

pron:jemand.tx: From Middle High German jeman, ieman, iemant, from Old High German ioman, eoman, equivalent to je + man.

noun:Joghurt.tx: Ottoman Turkish یوغورت (yōghurt, yoğurt) (cp. Turkish yoğurt). Cognate to English yogurt.

noun:Jasmin.tx: 16th century, from French jasmin, from Spanish jazmín, from Arabic ياسَمِين (yāsamīn), from Persian یاسمن (yâsaman). The pronunciation is spelling-based and thus only coincidentally very close to the Middle Eastern etyma. Use as a personal name following wider European usage since the 19th century.

noun:Juwel.tx: From late Middle Dutch jueel and its modern continuation in Dutch juweel. The Dutch word is borrowed from Old French jouel.

noun:Juwelier.tx: Probably from early modern Dutch juwelier, though the word is first attested in German. Analyzable as Juwel + -ier.

noun:Jenseits.tx: 18th-century nominalization of the adverb jenseits (“on that side”). Equivalent to jene (“that”) + Seite (“side”) + -s (adverbial suffix).

noun:Jahrzehnt.tx: 18th-century coinage displacing older ambiguous Dekade (“ten years; ten days”). From Jahr (“year”) + zehn (“ten”) with final -t probably on the model of older Jahrhundert (“century”), or possibly from zehnter (“tenth”). Compare Dutch jaartiental (“decade”).

noun:Judaismus.tx: From Late Latin Iūdaismus, from Koine Greek Ἰουδαϊσμός (Ioudaïsmós).

verb:jaulen.tx: Borrowed from German Low German [Term?]. Probably onomatopoetic, though a relation with gellen (“to shrill”) with common dialectal j- could be considered.

adj:jährlich.tx: From Middle High German jærlich, from Old High German jārlīh. By surface analysis, Jahr + -lich. Cognate with English yearly, Middle Dutch jaerlijc (Dutch jaarlijks).

adv:jährlich.tx: From Middle High German jærlich, from Old High German jārlīh. By surface analysis, Jahr + -lich. Cognate with English yearly, Middle Dutch jaerlijc (Dutch jaarlijks).

noun:Jänner.tx: From Middle High German jenner, an early borrowing from Latin Iānuārius. Compare the later borrowing Januar. Cognate with Pennsylvania German Yenner.

noun:Jahrbuch.tx: From Middle High German jārbuoch, from Old High German jārbuoh. Equivalent to Jahr (“year”) + Buch (“book”). Compare Low German Jårbook.

adj:jämmerlich.tx: From Middle High German jæmerlich, jæmerclich, jāmerlich, æmerlich, from Old High German jāmarlīh, āmarlīh. Equivalent to Jammer + -lich.

verb:jodeln.tx: From dialectal jo, expressing joy, of imitative origin.

noun:Jahrestag.tx: From Middle High German jārestac, from Old High German *jāres tag, from Proto-West Germanic *jāras dag, equivalent to Jahr (“year”) + -es- (“-'s”) + Tag (“day”).

noun:Jahrmarkt.tx: From Middle High German jārmarket, from Old High German jārmarkāt. Equivalent to Jahr (“year”) + Markt (“market”).

noun:Jurist.tx: From Middle High German juriste, borrowed from Medieval Latin jurista.

noun:Jahrgang.tx: From Jahr + Gang. Compare West Frisian jiergong.

adj:jiddisch.tx: From Yiddish ייִדיש (yidish), from Middle High German jüdesch, from Old High German judeisc, derived from judo, judeo + -isc, the former from Latin iūdaeus (“Judaean, Jew”), from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαῖος (Ioudaîos), derived from Ἰουδά (Ioudá, “Judah”) + -ιος (-ios), the former from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (yəhūḏāh). Doublet of jüdisch.

noun:Jungfernhäutchen.tx: Jungfer (“virgin”) + Häutchen (“membrane”); Häutchen is the diminutive of Haut (“skin”).

noun:Jüngling.tx: From Middle High German jungelinc, from Old High German jungiling, jungaling, jungeling, from Proto-Germanic *jungilingaz.

noun:Jolle.tx: From Low German jolle, from Middle Low German jolle, possibly ultimately from a Proto-Germanic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewlos (“tube”), see also Lithuanian aulas, Norwegian aul, Hittite [script needed] (auli-, “tube-shaped organ in the neck”), Albanian hollë, Latin alvus.

noun:Junkfood.tx: Unadapted borrowing from English junk food.

noun:Jonglieren.tx: Nominalisation of the German verb jonglieren.

noun:Jammertal.tx: From jammern + Tal, calque of Latin vallis lacrimarum.

noun:Jubiläum.tx: Borrowed from Late Latin iūbilaeum, from iūbilaeus.

noun:Jaspis.tx: From Middle High German jaspis, from Latin jaspis.

noun:Justiz.tx: 16th c., from Medieval Latin iūstitia (“justice, judiciary, jurisdiction”).

noun:Jux.tx: From Latin iocus with contraction. Attested since the 18th century, but likely older as it is widely attested in the dialects.

noun:Jünger.tx: From Middle High German jünger (“disciple, pupil, novice”), from Old High German jungiro (“apostle, disciple, pupil”, nominalised comparative of jung, literally “younger one”). Since Old High German its main use has been for the disciples of Christ, translating Latin discipulus.

intj:Jung.tx: The same as Junge with dialectal apocope.

noun:Jaguarundi.tx: Borrowed from Portuguese jaguarundi, from Paraguayan Guarani jaguarundi.

verb:jungen.tx: Compare Junges (“young of an animal, offspring”).

det:jeglicher.tx: Inherited from Middle High German ieclich, iegelich, from Old High German iogilīh, from Proto-West Germanic [Term?]. By surface analysis, je + gleich. Cognate with obsolete Dutch iegelijk.

noun:Jass.tx: Borrowed from Alemannic German Jass, from Dutch.

pron:jedweder.tx: From Middle High German ietweder, iegeweder.

det:jedweder.tx: From Middle High German ietweder, iegeweder.

noun:Jot.tx: From Latin iota, from Ancient Greek ἰῶτα (iôta), from Semitic yodh (the tenth letter of many Semitic alphabets), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *yad- (“hand”)

noun:Jury.tx: 18th century, from English jury, chiefly through French jury (whence the pronunciation).

adj:jährig.tx: From Middle High German jǣrec, from Old High German jārig, equivalent to Jahr + -ig.

noun:Jubel.tx: From Middle High German jūbel, from Latin iūbilus, from iūbilō (“to cheer, let out whoops”).

noun:Jeck.tx: Nominalisation of the adjective jeck (“crazy”). The word is the same as Geck (“dandy”) and is a Central Franconian (Ripuarian) form of it. Cognate to Dutch gek (“crazy”).

adj:jeck.tx: From Ripuarian Central Franconian, in which word-initial g- → j-. Doublet of German Geck (“dandy”). Also cognate with Dutch gek (“crazy”) and English geek.

noun:Jagdhund.tx: From Middle High German jagdhunt, jagethunt. Also attested as Middle High German jagehunt, jaghunt, and Old High German jagahund, jagahunt. Equivalent to Jagd + Hund.

noun:Jungfer.tx: Weakened form of Jungfrau (cf. Dutch juffer). Both words originally meant “unmarried (noble) woman” but have become semantically distinct. Compare Junker, constructed and reduced similarly.

noun:Jurte.tx: 17th century, from Russian ю́рта (júrta, “yurt”), from a Turkic language, from Proto-Turkic *yūrt (“dwelling place”).

verb:japsen.tx: Borrowed from German Low German [Term?]. Derived from jappen, which see for more.

verb:jauchzen.tx: From Middle High German jūchzen, derived from the interjection jūch (“yay, yahoo”). Compare Luxembourgish jäizen, Dutch juichen.

noun:Jambus.tx: Borrowed from Latin ïambus, from Ancient Greek ἴαμβος (íambos).

adj:jach.tx: From Middle High German gāch, related to jäh.

noun:Jus.tx: Borrowed from French jus, from Latin ius. Doublet of Jauche.

noun:Jett.tx: Borrowed from English jet. Doublet of Gagat.

noun:Jarmulke.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish יאַרמלקע (yarmlke), from Polish jarmułka, from Old Polish jałmurka.

verb:jubilieren.tx: From Middle High German jūbilieren, from Latin iūbilāre.

phrase:jemandem ist eine Laus über die L.tx: Literally, “a louse has walked over someone's liver”.

phrase:jemandem fällt ein Stein vom Herz.tx: Literally, “a stone falls from someone's heart”.

phrase:je später der Abend, desto schöne.tx: Literally, “the later the evening, the more beautiful (i.e. pleasant) are the guests”. Compare the same in Dutch hoe later op de avond, hoe schoner het volk.

adj:jungfräulich.tx: From Middle High German juncvröuwelich. By surface analysis, Jungfrau (“virgin”) + -lich (“-ly, -al”).

noun:Jawort.tx: From Middle High German jāwōrt. By surface analysis, Ja + Wort.

noun:Jungbrunnen.tx: From Middle High German juncbrunne. Equivalent to jung (“young”) + Brunnen (“well”).

verb:johlen.tx: From Middle High German jōlen (“to sing loudly”), of uncertain origin. Related to Middle Low German jolen, jȫlen (“to revel, exult, jubilate”), Dutch jolen (“to be excited, rejoice”). Possibly equivalent to jo + -len. Compare also Middle High German golen (“to sing, sing loudly”).

noun:Jobcenter.tx: Job + Center or English job center.

noun:Judenschule.tx: From Jude (“Jew”) + -n- + Schule (“school”). Compare Yiddish שול (shul, “synagogue”). The word Schule was also used by Luther to translate Ancient Greek συναγωγή (sunagōgḗ).

noun:Japse.tx: Shortened from Japaner or Japanese (which can explain the s and the e).

phrase:Jahr und Tag.tx: Originally a juristic term used in the Middle Ages. Compare Serbo-Croatian godinu dana.

intj:joa.tx: Alternative form and / or spelling of jo (“expresses agreement in a hesitant manner”).

phrase:jemandem stehen die Haare zu Berg.tx: Literally, “someone's hairs are raised [as if] to [become] mountains”. Compare English hair-raising.
